explanations.answer: The LORD heard his appeal for mercy
explanations.explanation: That's the reason, friend. He says, "I love the LORD, for He has heard my voice—my appeal for mercy." He doesn't start with a list of what he got. He starts with the fact that somebody listened when he cried out. I think that's the kind of love that sticks around.

explanations.answer: The LORD made him rich and respected
explanations.explanation: Money and respect are nice, but the psalm never brings them up. The reason he gives is that the LORD "…has heard my voice—my appeal for mercy." He loves the LORD because he was heard when he needed mercy. I'd take that over a fat bank account any day, and I'm a stamper whose first owner, Mother Miller, bought me for a quarter, so I know what I'm talking about.

explanations.answer: The LORD gave him a large family
explanations.explanation: A big family is a blessing, but this psalm doesn't mention one. His reason is right there in verse 1: the LORD "…has heard my voice—my appeal for mercy." He was heard, and that's why he loves Him. Keep your eyes on the first verse, baker, it answers its own question.

Careful, this one flips what he says. He says, "Because He has inclined His ear to me, I will call on Him as long as I live." Being heard doesn't end the praying for him. It's the reason he keeps it going. The LORD leaned in, so he plans to keep talking for life.

Right, it's the opposite. The psalmist says, "Because He has inclined His ear to me, I will call on Him as long as I live." He doesn't retire from prayer once he's been heard. He signs up for life. That's a man who found a good thing and isn't about to stop.

Yes, and the order matters. In verse 3 the ropes of death entangled him and the anguish of Sheol overcame him. Then he says, "Then I called on the name of the LORD: 'O LORD, deliver my soul!'" First the trouble, then the call.

It's true, friend. Verse 4 says, "Then I called on the name of the LORD: 'O LORD, deliver my soul!'" He does it while he's tangled in the ropes of death and overcome by the anguish of Sheol. The calling comes in the middle of the trouble, not after it.

explanations.answer: Gracious and righteous and full of compassion
explanations.explanation: That's his exact list: "The LORD is gracious and righteous; our God is full of compassion." Notice he says "our God" there, not just "my God." He got the mercy he begged for, and now he describes the LORD with these words. Gracious, righteous, compassionate. Hard to improve on that.

explanations.answer: Mighty and fearsome and full of glory
explanations.explanation: Those words sound big, but they're not his words here. He says, "The LORD is gracious and righteous; our God is full of compassion." He's describing the LORD he cried out to and was heard by. So the words he reaches for are gracious, righteous and compassionate.

explanations.answer: Holy and wise and full of majesty
explanations.explanation: Good words, but this psalm doesn't use them. Verse 5 says, "The LORD is gracious and righteous; our God is full of compassion." Those are the three words the psalmist gives. Holy and wise would be fine guesses, friend, but they aren't in this verse.

That's the one: "The LORD preserves the simplehearted; I was helpless, and He saved me." Look how he puts those two things side by side. He was helpless, and He saved me. That line makes me want to stand up in my apron and cheer.

Proud-hearted doesn't show up in this verse. He says, "The LORD preserves the simplehearted; I was helpless, and He saved me." The word he uses is simplehearted. Nice try, friend, but the verse names the simplehearted.

Not quite, friend. The verse says, "The LORD preserves the simplehearted; I was helpless, and He saved me." He's not bragging about being strong. He's saying he was helpless and was saved, and he names the simplehearted.

explanations.answer: The LORD has been good to it
explanations.explanation: Exactly. He says, "Return to your rest, O my soul, for the LORD has been good to you." His reason for rest is what the LORD has already done for him. I think it's a little like telling yourself to unclench after the oven timer finally goes off.

He doesn't say that at all. Just before, he talked about the ropes of death and the anguish of Sheol (Psalm 116:3). His reason for rest is this: "…for the LORD has been good to you." The trouble was real, and so was the goodness.

That's a fair thing to say in general, but it's not his reason. Verse 7 says, "Return to your rest, O my soul, for the LORD has been good to you." He bases his rest on the LORD's goodness, not on a rule about worrying.

Yes, tears. He says, "For You have delivered my soul from death, my eyes from tears, my feet from stumbling." He's talking straight to the LORD now, saying "You." The first blank is tears, and the list goes soul, eyes, feet.

Yes, stumbling. The verse says, "…my eyes from tears, my feet from stumbling." That's his whole list: soul, eyes and feet. And I'm a stamper who's been dropped on a kitchen floor, so I know how much that matters.
Blindness isn't in this verse. He says, "For You have delivered my soul from death, my eyes from tears, my feet from stumbling." His eyes were delivered from tears, so the first blank is tears.

Thorns don't show up in this verse. He says, "…my eyes from tears, my feet from stumbling." His feet were delivered from stumbling, so that's the second blank. Nice guess, friend, but the verse has its own words.

Sickness isn't in his list, friend. Verse 8 says, "For You have delivered my soul from death, my eyes from tears, my feet from stumbling." The psalm doesn't say what kind of trouble he had beyond what it names in verse 3. Stay with his words: tears and stumbling.

It's true. He says, "I will walk before the LORD in the land of the living." He was staring at death a few verses back (Psalm 116:3), and now he's making plans to keep walking. I think that's a man who knows what a gift his next step is.

It's true, baker. Verse 9 says, "I will walk before the LORD in the land of the living." After the ropes of death, he's talking about walking, and doing it before the LORD. That's quite a turn in six verses.

That's it: "In my alarm I said, “All men are liars!”" He tells us he said it when he was alarmed, and he doesn't hide it. I think that's honest of him. I've said some silly things when I was alarmed myself, mostly to a cookie tin.
Anger isn't the word he uses. He says, "In my alarm I said, “All men are liars!”" He was alarmed when it came out. It's a small difference, but the text gives us the exact word.
The psalm never says anything about old age. Verse 11 says, "In my alarm I said, “All men are liars!”" The moment he points to is his alarm, not his years.

Yes: "I will lift the cup of salvation and call on the name of the LORD." His answer to "How can I repay…" isn't a purchase. He lifts a cup and calls on the LORD's name. I'm relieved, because my budget is a quarter and a mustache.

He doesn't mention a shield. He says, "I will lift the cup of salvation and call on the name of the LORD." The cup of salvation is what he lifts, so a shield of victory isn't the answer. Nice try, friend.

No crown here, friend. Verse 13 says, "I will lift the cup of salvation and call on the name of the LORD." He lifts a cup of salvation. A crown would look great on a cookie box, but it's not in this verse.

Look again, because he says the opposite. Verse 14 says, "I will fulfill my vows to the LORD in the presence of all His people." That's out in the open, with everybody there. He's not planning to keep this one quiet.
Right. He says, "I will fulfill my vows to the LORD in the presence of all His people." Nothing quiet or hidden about that. He plans to do it in the presence of the LORD's people.

explanations.answer: Their death is valuable to Him
explanations.explanation: That's what "precious" is telling us. "Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of His saints." It means their death matters to Him, it's valuable in His sight. The psalm doesn't say more about it than that, so I'll let that line stand.

explanations.answer: He keeps His saints from ever dying
explanations.explanation: The verse doesn't say that. It says, "Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of His saints." That line speaks of their death, not of skipping it. It says their death is precious to Him.

explanations.answer: He gives His saints a long life
explanations.explanation: A long life might be nice, but that's not what this line says. It says, "Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of His saints." The word is precious, and it's about their death being valuable in His sight. This one is a heavy line, so I'll just say it plainly.

True. Verse 16 says, "Truly, O LORD, I am Your servant; I am Your servant, the son of Your maidservant; You have broken my bonds." He says "Your servant" twice, and then the bonds line lands. Notice who does the breaking: "You." Solid reading, baker!
It's true, friend. Verse 16 ends with "You have broken my bonds." It comes right after he says he's the LORD's servant twice. The servant lines and the broken bonds sit side by side.

Yes. He says, "I will offer to You a sacrifice of thanksgiving and call on the name of the LORD." He asked how to repay, and here's what he offers. It's a sacrifice of thanksgiving, with calling on the LORD's name right alongside it.

Atonement isn't the word in this verse. He says, "I will offer to You a sacrifice of thanksgiving and call on the name of the LORD." What he offers is thanks. It answers his own question about repaying.
Not mourning, baker. Verse 17 says, "I will offer to You a sacrifice of thanksgiving and call on the name of the LORD." He's been through sorrow, but the sacrifice he names is thanksgiving.

Yes, Jerusalem. He says, "…in the courts of the LORD’s house, in your midst, O Jerusalem. Hallelujah!" He talks to the city itself, like he's inviting it to listen. He wants his vows kept right where everyone can see.
Hebron isn't in this psalm. Verse 19 says, "…in the courts of the LORD’s house, in your midst, O Jerusalem." That's where he'll keep his vows, in the middle of Jerusalem.
Samaria doesn't appear here, friend. The psalm ends, "…in the courts of the LORD’s house, in your midst, O Jerusalem. Hallelujah!" Jerusalem is the city he names.
